To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the postprandial lipemia response to an oral fat tolerance tests was attenuated by acute exercise, undertaken 24 h prior to testing, when energy and CHO balance were restored.
acute exercise with a carbohydrate replacement to restore carbohydrate balance does not alter postprandial lipemia.
acute exhaustive exercise with and without CHO replacement influences postprandial lipemia, but only when the exercise is undertaken without CHO replacement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the body deals with food intake after exercise.
the effects of exercise on postpranded lipid metabolism.
understanding how acute exercise affects postprandial lipaemia, and the mechanisms underlying this effect.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
acute exercise with CHO replacement does not influence postprandial lipaemia.

the effects of acute exercise on postpr andial lipids are not clear cut and depend on many factors including the type, intensity and duration of exercise, and the extent to which CHO and energy balance are disrupted.
the benefits of acute exhaustive exercise, on postpr andial lipid metabolism are dependent on the magnitude of the CHO and energy deficit incurred.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
acute exhaustive exercise, undertaken on a fasting morning, may reduce postprandial lipemia and enhance postprandial high-density lipoproteins in healthy young men.

acute exercise, with or without carbohydrate replacement, does not influence postprandial insulin or glucose and that the influence on lipid metabolism depends on the extent of the associated energy deficit.
acute exercise with CHO replacement has little effect on postprandia lipid metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of acute exhaustive exercise, with and/or without CHO replacement, on the postprandial lipemic response may be overstated in studies that do not account for dietary compensation.
the benefits of acute exhaustive exercise for lipid metabolism are likely to be overstated when the effects of compensatory changes in energy and CHO balance are not accounted for.
exercise-induced changes in postpr andial TG may be overstated in studies that do not account for dietary compensation.
